name: Rosa Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Rosa, thanks for making time after a long day. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm a carpenter's labourer, second year, on a housing association site on the edge of town, four blocks of timber-frame flats going up where the old dye works used to be. I'm on the bus at ten past six, kettle in the site cabin by seven, then I'm carrying joists, cutting noggins, fixing plasterboard battens, whatever Pete the foreman points me at. I love the end of a day when a wall that wasn't there this morning is standing. What wears me out is the cold in my hands and being told twice how to do something I should already know.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what's hard about the money side?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Honestly, I like that it's real. I left school at sixteen, did a few years in a bakery, and this is the first job where I can point at a building and say I helped. Money's tight, though. I rent a flat over the laundrette on Mill Street with my partner Jonas, he's a care worker, and between us we've got maybe two weeks of bills put by. If I miss a week from rain or a bad back, we feel it straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. That's basically what my uncle Ray says every time it comes on the news. He's been on the tools thirty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, to be honest. In the cabin I'd say the robots never turned up and we're still the ones hanging doors in the sleet. Online I don't really post, but if I did I'd say the money should've gone into housing instead of chatbots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be relieved. I'm slow at this still, I know I am, and the last thing I need is the trade changing under me before I've even got good at it. If nothing changes, I've got time to learn it properly the old way, from Pete and Ray.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am. I'd keep going to the union branch meeting once a month at the Railway Club, finish my second year and push to get onto the trade certificate course the housing association half-pays for. I'd want to put twenty quid a week aside, but I know what usually happens to that twenty quid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. My worries would be the same old ones, the rent, the weather, my back. Nothing new on the pile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the twenty quid a week. What usually happens to it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The electric happens to it. Or Jonas's bus pass, or a pair of boots, because my last ones split at the toe in March. Pete wouldn't let me on the scaffold in trainers. So it's a nice idea, but I'm not going to pretend I'm a saver.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If AI barely changes anything, is there anything at work you'd still want to change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay, obviously, and the agency lads getting less than us for the same work, which isn't right. And proper heated drying rooms. None of that needs a computer, it needs the bosses to listen. That's what I'd still be pushing the branch on.

S0.say: I'd say I told you so and that the robots never turned up, while we're still the ones hanging doors in the sleet. If I posted at all, I'd say the money should have gone into housing instead of chatbots.
S0.think: I'd be relieved, because I'm still slow and still learning, and I don't want the trade changing before I've got good at it. If nothing changes, I get time to learn it the old way from people I trust.
S0.do: Carries on as normal, finishes her second year and pushes to get onto the half-paid trade certificate course. Keeps going to the monthly union branch meeting and would like to save twenty a week but doubts she will.
S0.feel: Calm and relieved. Her worries stay the familiar ones: rent, weather and her back.
S0.quote: The electric happens to it. Or Jonas's bus pass, or a pair of boots, because my last ones split at the toe in March.
S0.fieldNote: Rosa is proud that her work is physical and visible, and she's open about being slow and still learning. Her worries in this picture are the everyday ones of a low wage, not technology. She frames improvements in terms of the union and the bosses listening, not machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. That one sounds more like what the site managers talk about when they think we can't hear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need the union in on it from day one, not after. I'd say if a machine's doing the cutting, the people who did the cutting get first go at whatever new job comes with it. I'd say it to Pete's face, too, he knows where I stand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it scares me more than I'd let on. They already bring in wall panels made in a factory up the motorway, so we're half assembling, not building. If that grows, the bit of the job I'm on is the easy bit to take, the carrying and fixing, and I'm not quick on new gadgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the branch to ask for a written agreement about any new kit on our site, who's trained on it and whether anyone loses hours. I'd try to finish my certificate faster, maybe evening classes twice a week if they'd let me. I'd try to put away fifty a month instead of twenty, which means no takeaway on Fridays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, like when you hear something creak on a scaffold. Nothing's fallen yet, but you're listening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not quick on new gadgets. If the site brought in, say, a machine you had to run, how would you handle that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly at first, I'll be honest. I've still got a phone with a cracked screen and I don't use any of those AI apps, Jonas does all the online forms. I'd need someone to show me with their hands, not send me a video link. If they did that, I'd get there, slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on site would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kelvin, the other labourer. He's fifty-two, can't read well, and he's the best man with a wheelbarrow on that site. If the job turns into screens and forms, he's out first, and nobody's going to retrain a fifty-two-year-old who can't read the leaflet.

S1.say: We need the union in on this from day one, not after. If a machine's doing the cutting, the people who did the cutting get first go at whatever new job comes with it.
S1.think: It scares me more than I'd let on, because factory-made wall panels already take part of the work and my bit, the carrying and fixing, is the easiest to take. I'm not quick on new gadgets and I don't use AI apps.
S1.do: Gets her union branch to push for a written agreement on new equipment, training and hours. Tries to speed up her trade certificate with two evening classes a week and raise saving to fifty a month by cutting Friday takeaways.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like listening to a creaking scaffold. Nothing has gone wrong yet, but she's on alert.
S1.quote: If the job turns into screens and forms, he's out first, and nobody's going to retrain a fifty-two-year-old who can't read the leaflet.
S1.fieldNote: Her public line is confident and union-led, while privately she admits real fear about factory-made panels. She worries as much about an older colleague as about herself. Resistance to technology is real but not total: she'd learn if taught by hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. I'd barely have my certificate by then. Sorry, give me a second.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be angry out loud. I'd say this is a handful of rich men in another country deciding we don't need to eat, and the government standing there letting it happen. I'd be at every protest going, and I'd say that at work and down the Railway Club.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd think I'm done. I'm junior, I'm slow, I've got two weeks of money and there's hardly any other building work round here as it is. If a robot can carry and fix and doesn't get cold hands, why would anyone keep me on, even with the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd cancel the gym and the phone contract and go to pay-as-you-go. I'd get the branch to demand a guaranteed income for anyone pushed out, and I'd sign up for the strike fund. If I lost the job, I'd be at my mum's in Ashby with Jonas on the sofa bed within three months, because there's nothing else I could afford.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick. Like I've missed a step on the stairs in the dark. I wouldn't be sleeping, I know that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Some people would say that with two years' notice, she should learn something new quickly. What would you say to that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn what, though? If it can do almost any job, what am I racing towards? I'm not going to win a race against a thing that never sleeps by doing an online course on a cracked phone. I'd rather spend the two years fighting for a decent deal for everyone than pretending I can outrun it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Jonas the night you heard it was coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say we'll be all right, which would be a lie. Then I'd say his job's safer than mine, because who wants a robot wiping their nan, and he'd say don't be so sure. And then we'd sit there and work out how long the money lasts, which wouldn't take long.

S2.say: This is a handful of rich men in another country deciding we don't need to eat, and the government is standing there letting it happen. I'll be at every protest going.
S2.think: I think I'm done: junior, slow, two weeks of money and hardly any other building work round here. Even the union couldn't keep me on against a robot that never gets cold hands.
S2.do: Cancels her gym and phone contract straight away and pushes her branch to demand a guaranteed income for displaced workers. Joins the strike fund and expects to move into her mum's house in Ashby with Jonas within three months of losing her job.
S2.feel: Sick and shaken, as if she'd missed a step in the dark. She expects not to sleep.
S2.quote: I'm not going to win a race against a thing that never sleeps by doing an online course on a cracked phone.
S2.fieldNote: This is where Rosa's thin cushion and resistance to change meet: she sees no option except fighting collectively and falling back on family. She rejects retraining as pointless rather than frightening. She blames tech owners and government, and is honest that she'd lie to her partner to comfort him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit more breathing room, but not much. I'd be thirty-two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message, louder and earlier. I'd say we've got five years to make the government put rules on this and make the companies pay for whoever they push out. I'd be the one handing out leaflets at the site gate, which Pete would love.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think five years just means I'd see it coming for longer. I'd get my certificate, maybe get decent, and then watch the thing I got good at go. That might be worse than two years, in a way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every branch meeting and probably stand as the site rep, which I've been avoiding. I'd write to our MP, the first letter I've ever written to anyone like that. I'd try to get a few months of rent put by, a hundred a month, by selling my bike and doing Saturday cash jobs with Ray, hanging doors in people's houses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bad. I'd be lying awake doing sums most nights, I know I would. At least I'd have something to do with my hands about it, which helps a little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be doing Saturday jobs with Ray. Isn't that also work a robot could take by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yeah. But old ladies who want a door hung aren't going to buy a robot the first year, are they? That cash keeps us going while the big sites change. I'm not saying it's a plan forever, it's a plan for a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you'd avoid learning new things in the fast one. With five years, would you try anything new?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe something with people, like a support worker, like Jonas. I'd rather that than learn to babysit a robot on a site. But I'd only do it if the union or the council paid for the course, because I can't afford to lose wages for it.

S3.say: We've got five years to make the government put rules on this and make the companies pay for whoever they push out. I'd be handing out leaflets at the site gate.
S3.think: Five years just means I'd see it coming for longer. I'd finally get decent at the trade and then watch it go, which might be worse than two years in a way.
S3.do: Stands as site union rep, writes her first ever letter to her MP, and saves a hundred a month by selling her bike and doing Saturday cash jobs hanging doors with her uncle. Would consider training as a support worker only if the union or council paid.
S3.feel: Losing sleep over money and the future, though having practical things to do helps a little.
S3.quote: I'd get my certificate, maybe get decent, and then watch the thing I got good at go.
S3.fieldNote: She sees extra warning time as a longer wait rather than a chance, which fits her resistance. Still, five years shifts her from despair to organising and side jobs. She'd only consider care work, not tech work, and only if someone else funds it. Mood set at alarmed because her own words describe constant pressure and losing the skill she's working for, with only stopgap plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. Okay. That's a different feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do it properly, so there's no excuse. Rules, retraining on full pay, a share of what the robots make going back to people. I'd say it calmly for once, because there'd be time to win the argument.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think ten years gives me a real chance to get good, earn a bit more and maybe save, then deal with it. By then I might be on proper trade rates. It's still the same ending, I know, but I'm not at the ending yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going on site and get my certificate in the next two years. I'd stay site rep and push the branch to get a deal in writing with the housing association before any robots come. And I'd set up a standing order, small, forty a month, into an account I can't see on my phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can live with. More like a job I know is coming than a car about to hit me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you'd rather fight than try to outrun it. With ten years, does that change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. With ten years I'd fight and get my certificate, not one or the other. I still wouldn't sit at a computer learning code, that's not me. But getting proper at carpentry, yeah, because the people who'll last longest are the ones who can do the fiddly old stuff in old houses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you look ahead to 2036, what do you picture on a normal day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't really know, I can't picture it. Maybe me doing repair jobs in terraced houses that are too awkward for a machine, and doing union stuff. Maybe I'm wrong and I'm on the sofa. I'd rather not guess further than that.

S4.say: Ten years is enough time to do it properly, so there's no excuse. Rules, retraining on full pay, and a share of what the robots make going back to people.
S4.think: Ten years gives me a real chance to get good, reach proper trade rates and maybe save first. It's the same ending, I know, but I'm not at the ending yet.
S4.do: Keeps working on site and finishes her trade certificate within two years. Stays as union site rep pushing for a written deal with the housing association, and sets up a forty-a-month standing order into a hidden savings account.
S4.feel: Anxious but manageable, like a known job coming rather than a car about to hit her.
S4.quote: With ten years I'd fight and get my certificate, not one or the other.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years is the first picture where she combines fighting with improving her own skills. She still rules out computer-based retraining and bets on fiddly repair work in old houses. She is honest that she can't picture 2036 and won't guess.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easily. Because I'd have nothing, no money, no skill that's finished, nowhere to go but my mum's. What would help is the government guaranteeing a wage if they let this happen, a proper one, not forms and queues, and the union being at the table before the machines arrive, not after.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who's going to build the houses for everyone who's lost their job. We've got a waiting list of four thousand for council flats round here. If the robots really can build, fine, build those first. Then I'd believe it was for us.

headlineQuote: If the robots really can build, fine, build those first. Then I'd believe it was for us.
portrait: Rosa Larsen is a 27-year-old carpenter's labourer in her second year on a housing association site, living with her care-worker partner over a laundrette with about two weeks of savings. She's union-minded, proud of physical work and frank about being slow and still learning, and she never uses AI tools. If AI stalls she's relieved; in steady change she organises and worries about an older colleague. The fast AGI picture leaves her panicked with nowhere to go but her mum's, while five and ten years shift her towards organising, side jobs and finishing her trade certificate, though she still won't retrain into tech.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she'd have no savings, no finished skill and nowhere to go except her mum's house.
whatWouldHelp: A government-guaranteed proper wage without forms and queues, and the union at the table before machines arrive.
